# Committed training trajectories make data review consequential {#sec-training-audits}

Public training code and a claimed dataset do not show that a released
checkpoint resulted from them. The proposed additional evidence is a binding
record of the training trajectory, with randomly selected updates replayed by
the reviewer. Deterministic seed sampling here specifies the **training-data
draws**; the reviewer's choices of updates to inspect use separate, private
randomness. The attacker may know the published verification procedure.
This review requires access to sampled checkpoint states and data, even if
ordinary users receive only API access.

This setting has direct predecessors. Jia et al.'s Proof-of-Learning records
training evidence for replay-based checks [@jia2021learning]. Choi, Shavit, and
Duvenaud's Proof-of-Training-Data specifically addresses which data produced
the weights, using transcripts, seed commitments, replay, and additional
tests. Their proposed efficient checks are explicitly heuristic rather than
a proved solution against all feasible adversaries [@choi2023trainingdata].
The following is a minimal accounting model for a trajectory audit, not a new
cryptographic protocol or a claim to resolve that paper's security problem.

Let $s_i$ contain the complete training state at update $i$: weights, optimizer
state, and any other state needed for exact replay. Given approved training
code $U$, committed data $D$, and training seed $r$, define
$$
d_i=\operatorname{Draw}(D,r,i),\qquad
s_{i+1}=U(s_i,d_i,r,i).
$$
The seed also determines other stochastic choices, or these are separately
committed. Pin the initialization or its verified ancestry, preprocessing,
loss, schedule, and numerical execution semantics. A seed alone does not make
parallel floating-point execution reproducible.

Before audit choices are revealed, bind the ordered states and data identities
in a hash commitment, authenticate it, and bind its last weights to the
released artifact. A hash chain or Merkle commitment can prevent changing
records after a challenge under the appropriate cryptographic assumptions;
signatures identify who endorsed them. Neither proves that an update was
executed correctly. Blockchain consensus is unnecessary if an independent
reviewer or append-only log already fixes the commitment. The reviewer obtains
the authenticated states and actual consumed data for selected updates, checks
their membership, and replays $U$. Unavailable records fail the check.
An efficient encoding of evolving data intake remains an implementation
question; a hash without available data is not an exposure audit.

**Proposition 4 (random transition checks).** Fix a transcript of $T$ updates
containing $m$ invalid transitions under an exact replay predicate. If the
reviewer samples $q$ distinct updates uniformly without replacement, the
probability of accepting every sampled transition is
$$
\frac{\binom{T-m}{q}}{\binom{T}{q}}
\leq (1-m/T)^q\leq e^{-qm/T},
$$
with zero numerator when $q>T-m$.

*Proof.* Of the $\binom{T}{q}$ equally likely samples, exactly
$\binom{T-m}{q}$ contain only valid transitions. For $q\leq T-m$, each factor
$(T-m-j)/(T-j)$ is at most $1-m/T$; the remaining cases are immediate.
$\square$

Thus a guaranteed invalid fraction $\rho$ is caught with probability at least
$1-\delta$ using $q\geq\log(1/\delta)/\rho$ checks, when that many checks are
available; checking all $T$ catches any invalid transition. But one invalid
transition is detected with probability only $q/T$. Subsequent transitions
can be consistent with an incorrect starting state. This counting bound alone
does not connect invalid-transition count to final behavioral harm. Exact verification
of every transition, from the approved initial state to the released endpoint,
does establish the specified trajectory by induction. It does not establish a
unique physical history: other computations may lead to the same artifact.

This also bounds what random checking can guarantee against concentrated
errors. For any sampling design with expected budget $q$, the sum of the
$T$ inclusion probabilities is $q$. At least one update therefore has
inclusion probability no greater than $q/T$. Uniform sampling equalizes this
worst-case coverage without assuming the reviewer can recognize a risky update
in advance. Additional integrity tests may improve on this restricted audit.
The coverage argument alone does not establish that a harmful transcript can
be constructed at the least-sampled position without changing those tests.

## Cheap checks can constrain the unchecked transitions

A useful hybrid audit applies cheap checks to every committed transition and
recomputes gradients for a private random subset. Cheap checks can enforce
parameter-step limits, optimizer-state ranges, schedule and counter integrity,
and consistency of the optimizer recurrence with a claimed gradient. With
$P$ parameters, reading and checking vector states costs at least order $P$
per step; storage and transfer may dominate even when this is cheaper than
backpropagation. These checks must cover the whole transcript, not just the
sample, to support a global bound on unchecked steps.

The threat of interest is a sparse set of gradients computed using smuggled,
undeclared data or an undeclared loss. Such gradients can follow learned
features toward a desired behavior while the logged weights and optimizer
states obey the optimizer equations. Their provenance is false even when
their norms look ordinary. Direct weight or state edits need not arise from
any gradient; checking the recurrence excludes some of these edits, but
checking a recurrence against an unverified claimed gradient does not verify
the declared objective. Gradient scaling, clipping, accumulation, and the
loss itself belong to the committed computation.

Related results establish reasons to investigate sparse interventions, not
that this particular hybrid audit is defeated. Qi et al. report safety
degradation from fine-tuning on small sets of examples
[@qi2023finetuning]; example count is not invalid-update count. Bagdasaryan
et al. demonstrate model replacement and evasion of selected anomaly checks
in federated learning [@bagdasaryan2019backdoor]. A federated client update
can aggregate many local steps; it is not a verified centralized gradient.
Neither result establishes a general relation between an ordinary-looking
update and its eventual behavioral effect. The optimizer models in
@sec-optimizer-memory isolate that missing relation.

Costs include retaining replayable states and data, committing them, and
recomputing selected updates. With comparable per-update costs and directly
available states, $q$ replays add approximately $q/T$ of the original update
compute, excluding storage, transfer, and commitment costs. Storing only
segment checkpoints trades storage for longer replay; Proposition 4 then
counts invalid segments, not individual updates. A tolerant numerical check
certifies only its chosen tolerance relation, not exact global equivalence.

Training-data review is now tied to the inspected trajectory, subject to these
verification limits. It can reveal explicitly malicious teaching examples or
undeclared sources. A completely valid trajectory can nevertheless learn an
unwanted policy from declared data. Approved code must therefore mean an
inspected update rule, not merely available source. This evidence complements
behavioral auditing; it does not turn training provenance into an alignment
certificate.

## Full coverage need not mean full recomputation

Trusted execution is an alternative to trusting sampled replay. NVIDIA's
attestation documentation describes verification of genuine devices and
firmware and protected execution [@nvidia2026attestation]. A training
certificate would additionally need an attested program that binds approved
code, initialization, consumed data, randomness, optimizer state, and final
weights throughout execution. The CPU, accelerators, communication paths, and
restart logic must lie within the stated trust boundary. A protected signer
that merely signs a trainer-supplied log does not supply this guarantee.
Verifying such a certificate can avoid repeating training, conditional on
the hardware and software trust assumptions; this is not a trust-free proof.

Algebraic verification can also check more computation than it recomputes.
Slalom uses Freivalds-style randomized checks of outsourced linear algebra
inside a trusted-execution design, demonstrating neural inference and
explicitly discussing unresolved training costs [@tramer2019slalom]. Such
checks use hidden verifier randomness across arithmetic operations rather
than leaving whole training steps unexamined. Training also requires binding
the dataflow, nonlinear operations, and numerical representation.
Cryptographic training proofs such as zkDL offer another route
[@sun2023zkdl]. A fast verifier does not imply cheap proof generation;
none of these citations establishes a production-scale LLM training
certificate at a specified overhead.
